MarketWatch: A new report from Cambridge, MA-headquartered independent research boutique Forrester Research scrutinized the financial health of the major AI players and concluded that while a bursting of the AI bubble is not imminent, signs of strain are showing.

Their research illustrates that until September nearly all of the capital investment was paid for through operating cash but since then, the cushion is wearing thin. For example, Amazon spent $77 billion versus $42 billion of cash. Alphabet blew $9 billion more than available cash, Meta by $1.12 billion and both companies sold shares to raise capital in the last few months. Microsoft is still spending its own cash but borrowed money anyway through a filing ro raise $25 billion in bonds.

More worryingly, on the fringes of this cohort Oracle spent $1.61 per operating dollar in the year to August. The Forrester report, lead-authored by Brian Hopkins, defines a bubble as “supply built ahead of demand”. They estimate U.S. GDP needs to rise by 5% by 2035 to justify the current level of infrastructure investment.

But perhaps the biggest notable from the ADP report was job-changers’ gross pay growth jumped to 7.6%, the fastest since March 2024, but it was not just about base pay.

“Employers of all sizes were hiring last month, and our data suggests that job-changers were lured by a combination of bonuses, overtime, and more hours in addition to higher base pay,” said Nela Richardson, ADP’s chief economist.

Consistent with that, ADP’s base pay measure, which strips out those extras, shows a much smaller gain for job-changers, at 4.8%, and 3.0% for job-stayers. So the extra money for people switching jobs is coming mostly through bonuses and hours, not higher wage rates.

It fits with Tuesday’s JOLTS report, where quits, a gauge of workers’ confidence in finding another job, hit their highest since March 2025.

Various commentary from Qualcomm, Arm, to Meta executives this week during the AI selloff: 

$LITE CEO: "You had a comment from the CEO of $IREN and I'd second that. There's a massive disconnect in what we're seeing in our demand books. 

And what the markets are showing. And yet you're seeing a massive, massive selloff." (Fri, Nov 6)

$AMD CEO CNBC: "We're at the very beginning of the adoption cycle, where people can see where AI and superintelligence will take us" 

"We are seeing demand being higher than supply" (Wed, Nov 4)

$ARM CEO regarding a debate whether AI infrastructure spending is about to peak:

"I think in some states where it gets harder, other states may pick it up to make it easier, but I do believe strongly that if the US hesitates in any way shape performance in terms of data center buildout...

"The rest of the world is ready and willing. There is just huge demand for this capacity. And I think globally the US really wants to be able to compete against China. China is not slowing down at all." (Thu, Nov 5)

$APLD CEO: Bank construction lending, project financing and bond markets remain available, although interest rates and credit spreads have risen

"The big risk is delivering on time." "The demand picture is extremely robust." (Mon, Nov 2)

$QCOM CEO: "It's not demand bound. It's a supply bound." 

"We're short on wafers, we're short on substrate, we're short on assembly. Everything is short because demand is very, very high." 

"I think what the market is reacting to is what is the speed of the compute build out."

$META on political risk: "We did have a governor that won last night who did make data centers a big part of the platform.

Say as soon as we get past the inauguration, let's meet because we don't want to lose this investment in our town. We don't want these jobs to go elsewhere." (Wed, Nov 4)

Even politicians campaigning against data centers are negotiating. But Meta's president also emphasized that starting new US DCs will become more difficult. 

TLDR:
-> Extremely bullish commentary from accelerator players, networking, and semi companies
-> DC developers report strong pricing/demand, but increasingly emphasize financing, permitting and execution risks (more cautious)
-> Politicians that previously campaigned against DCs are showing cooperation

There's an important difference between demand disappearing and demand being delayed by the inability to build fast enough.

Despite the severity of the selloff, I'm not seeing evidence of widespread AI demand destruction in commentary.

or single digit memory companies with contracted demand + price floors years out and say that's a bubble?

- Certain startups like Instinct that look like a private valuation bubble. 
- Leveraged Neoclouds that didn't finance properly
- and AI lab valuations and commitments, which should be viewed cautiously.

- Optical companies like $POET traded -$97M under net cash. Valuing the operating business very negatively, not even at $0. 

- While AI companies with larger premiums continue to record demand over the next 3-5 years. Such as the new $20B LTAs signed w/ $COHR to $5B LTAs signed w/ $LITE. 

Can someone in the media honestly see negative EV high-beta optical companies, where 2 years of burnrate would still value the company below $0.  

or single digit memory companies with contracted demand + price floors years out and say that's a bubble?

Many of these names are extremely profitable today... 

But obviously there's other elements inside the theme, such as: 

- Certain startups like Instinct that look like a private valuation bubble. 
- Leveraged Neoclouds that didn't finance properly
- and AI lab valuations and commitments, which should be viewed cautiously. 

But everything gets grouped into one with the boogyman of "leverage" or "debt". 

Yes, valuations can compress or correct from macro, potential regulatory uncertainty, or potential capex reductions. 

But for the companies physically powering the AI buildout, it looks more like the Great AI Deleveraging of 2026... 

Than anything like fundamental demand destruction.

As more earnings come out and free cash flow accumulates over time.

I'm confident in a recovery, especially in bottlenecks, and for markets to eventually discern durability + growth over frothy valuations tied to AI.

There's never been a more interesting time in institutional digital assets, and never a harder time to tell what's real. Every week brings another wave of announcements.

So I've been mapping the relationships behind them: who issues, who custodies, who settles, who supervises, and who just signed the press release. The map now covers 672 initiatives and 1,043 organizations and networks, with roughly 3,200 links across announced projects, pilots and live services.

What it shows, as of this week:

• Settlement and market infrastructure is the largest category tracked, at 176 initiatives. The plumbing is a major focus, with DTCC, BNY, Chainlink and Securitize featuring prominently.

• Digital money and payments is next, with 154 initiatives spanning stablecoins, tokenized deposits, wholesale central-bank money and the infrastructure supporting them. Circle and HSBC feature prominently alongside Citi, Standard Chartered, JPMorgan and Swift. Visa and Mastercard are each linked to around a dozen initiatives. Projects such as the BIS’s Project Agorá and Swift’s shared ledger show institutions coming together to build common infrastructure.

• Organizations classified as traditional finance outnumber crypto-native firms by roughly five to four in the map. The incumbents are active participants: HSBC, BNY, JPMorgan, Citi and Standard Chartered appear alongside Circle, Ondo Finance and Securitize across the relationships captured so far.

• Institutional digital assets span private infrastructure and public networks. Permissioned platforms remain important for wholesale banking and settlement, while Ethereum and networks including Solana, Canton, Stellar, Base and Avalanche support a range of institutional applications.

• Policy has its own layer: 38 regulatory developments, from the SEC’s innovation exemption to Hong Kong’s first stablecoin licences. Oversight relationships are shown separately from project participation.

The map is a growing record of documented relationships, rather than a definitive ranking of market activity. Many entries were added or updated in the past two weeks. Behind each institution and initiative is a deeper profile: what it is building, who it works with, what role it plays and the latest reported developments.

The announcements are the starting point. Following the connections makes the market easier to understand.

If you invest in growth stocks like those John Lupton once promoted and Shay Boloor (reportedly down 35% YTD) now promotes, understand what you’re signing up for. Perhaps only one in ten growth stocks will ever deliver, while portfolio drawdowns of 30%, 50%, or even 60% are very real possibilities.

Shay himself admitted only yesterday that he started trading growth stocks just three years ago. Many of the names he promotes have reportedly fallen 30% to 80%, some even 90%. Of course, he wasn’t going to tell you to sell at the peak. And I don’t entirely blame him. How much skill can anyone develop in just three years?

The real problem is people blindly following paid stock promoters without demanding a verifiable long-term track record.

Over the weekend, we saw performance figures published for several subscription services turned money managers. Even Hedgeye has reportedly underperformed the index since inception, and by a considerable margin, despite constantly mocking both Scandinavian fund managers and CMTs who have struggled to beat the market themselves.

The Scandinavian fund managers and economists turned money managers are discovering that producing sophisticated analysis and uploading beautiful charts are two very different things from actually making money. As for CMTs, has anyone ever seen one with a verifiable long-term track record of beating the market? I certainly haven’t.

All former market heroes. Smart writing, impressive presentations, and pretty charts don’t equal superior returns.

I have nothing personal against these people. They seem nice, and nobody forced anyone to subscribe. But when you charge for investment services, you open yourself up to public scrutiny. People have every right to question what you’re selling and whether it’s worth paying for.

Let’s not pretend that if your portfolio is down 35% YTD while the Nasdaq is up 7%, everything is fine. It’s not. You underestimated the risks.

Nobody willingly signs up to make 100% one year only to lose 30%, 50%, or more the next. Losing a third of your savings is devastating, particularly when there’s no guarantee you’ll ever recover it.

And here’s the fundamental difference between investing in broad indices and individual growth stocks. Historically, the $SPX and $QQQ have eventually recovered from major drawdowns and reached new highs. Future recovery isn’t guaranteed, but the historical record is clear.

Individual growth stocks are another story. Many of those that collapsed in 2021 still haven’t recovered five years later. Some never will. Others that collapsed recently may not recover by 2030, if ever. The index can recover while your stocks never do.

Even if you’re down 90%, selling can still be the right decision. Your purchase price is irrelevant to what a business is worth today.

We don’t invest for sport. We do it to feed our families, build a better future, and achieve our dreams. The average investor deserves to understand these risks before putting hard-earned savings into someone’s stock picks.

I suppose it’s human nature to follow false gods, false prophets, false messiahs, and cling to false promises and false hopes.

Despite all the jokes and sarcasm on X, this is not a game. This is real money, real lives, and real consequences.

Hope is not a strategy.

Do We Even Want to Own Individual Stocks Anymore?

I like to reflect on things as they happen and be brutally harsh with myself, analyzing my returns, my losses, and the lessons I’ve learned. It’s equally important to distinguish where I made money because I had a genuine edge and where I was simply lucky.

Looking at 2026, some of the world’s most sophisticated hedge funds, employing the best analysts with enormous resources, are down YTD, and most have underperformed the index.

It makes me wonder, especially after watching $INTC collapse 30% in a single day, whether we should even bother owning individual stocks, particularly large companies that everyone follows and where others have vastly more resources than we do.

The more I contemplate this, the more I believe we should limit individual stock investments to perhaps four or five exceptional opportunities a year, where we have a genuine edge.

I’m talking about special situations: $AMZN falling toward $200 during a macro selloff, $ZIM trading below its cash value, $WGS following its earnings selloff, $STAA following its buyout offer, shorting $UVXY when volatility reaches extreme levels, or buying oil options when the U.S. is assembling a massive military force. There may also be occasional opportunities in overlooked small caps.

Another lesson: Stay away from speculative growth stocks. If 2021 didn’t teach you that, perhaps 2026 will. Any company being sold as “the future of something” without strong earnings to back it up is a speculative growth stock. Buying lottery tickets cannot be an investment strategy.

I don’t know a single growth stock investor who consistently told you the right time to get in and, more importantly, the right time to get out. Just look at the subscription sellers promoting growth stocks, some of whom are reportedly down 30% YTD. Can you afford that kind of drawdown? I don’t think you can.

And to all of you who love speculative growth stocks that can double or lose most of their value, be brutally honest with yourselves. Net net, are you actually up or down on these lottery tickets? Forget the fantasy, the occasional 100% winner, and the stocks you conveniently forget to mention. Look at your entire P&L. Are you making money or losing money? No fantasies.

Outside these special situations, why take single-stock risk? If I believe technology will outperform, I can simply own $QQQ. If I like a particular sector, I can own a sector ETF and avoid waking up to a 30% collapse in one of my holdings.

Suppose I offered you an investment with a 50% chance of gaining 30% tomorrow and a 50% chance of losing 30%. Would you really want to own it?

I’ve already significantly reduced my individual stock recommendations in 2026, and I intend to reduce them even further in 2027.

I doubt I’ll make more than four or five individual stock or special situation recommendations next year. Even if 2027 turns out to be an exceptionally opportunistic year, I expect to publish no more than six write-ups on investment ideas that I consider truly exceptional.

The rest of the time, I believe it’s probably smarter to own index ETFs. Not necessarily broad market indices. Sector ETFs can be just as useful when I have a strong view on a particular industry.

Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

# 1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed

Let us re-cap the economic theory behind valuation of a fee-burning token. This is the "net present value" (NPV) theory.

Formula: market cap = fees burned / discount rate

Imagine you have a token of which $1 billion is burned per year, and this is a long-term stable equilibrium. Now, imagine the discount rate is 4%; that is, people value having $1B today as much as $1.04B in one year.

The idea is that $1B / 4% = $25B serves as a natural "floor" for the valuation: if the valuation drops lower than that, then someone could buy an asset expected to pay $1 per year forever for less than $25 (by buying some tokens, and then selling >4% of their supply each year so their share of the total pie remains the same), and so by buying the asset you reliably beat the market.

In 2021-23, Ethereum burned millions of ETH per year in this way.

But here's the problem: this was never a true floor. The reason is that the bulk of that burn was crypto-internal use cases. If ETH had dropped by 10x, then the profits from those use cases would have also dropped, because all the buyers would have had much less money to pay with. This applies both to things like that infamous $180m-fees-burned-in-one-day digital monkey sale (yes, this happened; if you don't remember look it up!), and to more "normal" things like lending. The floor argument only works if the backing of the revenue stream is external.

Today, Ethereum actually has a better claim to this external backing, because of the growing RWA economy, but on the other hand, perhaps precisely because it's a normal stable mature business, it's not going to randomly go crazy and burn $180m on a digital monkey sale.

2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand compromising decentralization and capture resistance

If we decide we actually want to optimize ETH for burning fees to justify a present-day ~$270B market cap, then Ethereum would essentially be functioning as a world-scale major corporation - it would be somewhere around L'Oreal (#55).

Now, what do *real* major corporations have to do in order to maintain their positions in the long term?

1. They spend. AI estimates L'Oreal as spending ~0.58% of its market cap per year on R&D. This would bankrupt the EF almost immediately. So this would require in-protocol funding to the tune of ~700k ETH per year, with all the political issues that it entails (so validator revenue would get cut by 2/3). And that's just R&D. Corporations have to spend on all kinds of things beyond just cranking out more units of their pre-existing product.
2. They govern. To survive new waves of technology and culture, you have to make highly opinionated choices to go after new markets, make new kinds of products with new features to appeal to people who think in new ways and use the newest technologies. Ethereum would need to have highly interventionist governance, for the long term.

Needless to say, both of these are far from conducive to optimizing capture resistance and decentralization.

On top of this there is another concern: optimizing for fee burning means optimizing for high gas prices to some degree. This may price out users, including some users who may need privacy and security the most. The price that maximizes price * usage leads to less usage than the price that allows as much usage as possible subject to safe blockchain resource limits.

3. Optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with decentralization and CROPS

Whenever I ask what people appreciate the most about Ethereum (as opposed to either other blockchains, or anything outside the blockchain world), the most common answer is: decentralization and CROPS (censorship and capture resistance, open source, privacy and security).

Decentralization and CROPS have a lot of value, even to institutions. For individuals, privacy is often viewed as an abstract ideology. For institutions, it's prudent risk management, data protection law compliance, and a number of other things. Likewise for security. And likewise for running your own node (enterprise buzzword: "on-prem deployment").

But what about for the ETH holder? Well, it depends why you're an ETH holder. If you want ETH to optimally chase financial trends and collect fees from them, then you want a Fearless Leader™ who bravely shouts on the socials that Ethereum loves [insert opportunity here] and will pragmatically reconfigure itself to give it explicit protocol support.

But if your primary reason to hold ETH is as an SoV, then you will be judging ETH by SoV-ish metrics. And what is the first and most important SoV-ish metric?

To survive.

That's what a big chunk of this last Devcon was about ("post-quantum and post-AI"). You want a chain that is taking conservative tradeoffs ("hash-only security, all formally proven, >3x more rounds than known to be necessary for security"). You want a chain that is aiming for at least partial ossification, where the great balance of work will move to higher levels of the stack once the core is complete. You want a chain that aims to minimize protocol politics, by having a very high bar before it accepts either precompiles that bloat the protocol or new kinds of in-protocol rewards that could get captured.

What other SoV'ish metrics?

The ability to easily hold it safely (hence, work on multisigs).
The ability to hold it privately (hence, kohaku work).
The ability to hold it privately *and* safely (hence, 8288 and private-AA workstreams already starting).
The guarantee that if you have coins, you can send them, and block builders can't stop you (FOCIL)
Minimized infrastructure dependence (basically the whole decentralization roadmap, including the fact that I am able to currently run a node on this laptop, and it synced in < 6 hours and takes up only 1/8 of my hard drive - better stats than in 2019!)

Now, are there "adoption" goals that are highly synergistic with SoV?

Very much so.

The more assets there are natively issued on L1, including both RWAs and native decentralized assets, the larger a set of things you can "do" with your ETH, the better. Being able to easily (including safely, trustlessly) convert back and forth between ETH and other assets, use ETH as collateral to do things with other assets, etc, all forms part of the utility of holding ETH.

There are still some conflicts between serving these use cases and decentralization (eg. we want to be careful about fast slots and impact on centralization), but on the whole much less than what you get if you maximize fees.

Conclusion:

The best social reason to care about Ethereum is because it makes decentralization and CROPS properties a reality for more people and uses.

The best private reason to hold ETH is its SoV properties, which are a direct consequence of that decentralization and CROPS.

correct, this is the stablecoin trilemma (made up term, dont think anyone ever wrote this down):

between three properties of 
1) crypto-backed/immutable
2) solvent
3) scalable,
a stablecoin can only choose 2 of 3. 

old-dai, lusd chose 1+2 (sacrifice scalability)
usdt, usdc choose 2+3 (sacrifice immutability)
terrausd and its many clones chose 1+3 (sacrifice solvency)

note that the three choices not equal: 
- a stablecoin that isnt solvent fails its single most important test.
- give that money's utility scales with its network, sacrificing scalability is a large price that ultimately dooms the coin to failure
- immutability, then, is arguably the least-bad thing to sacrifice, because ("the only free lunch") it can be at least partially addressed with diversification. you also become less vulnerable with scale (see tether being a huge holder of t-bills giving it a certain political immunity)
